concepts.title: Thermal Equilibrium and the Zeroth Law
concepts.definition: Bodies left in contact stop exchanging net heat when their temperatures match -- thermal equilibrium. The zeroth law extends this: if two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other, which is exactly the property that makes temperature a measurable, comparable quantity.
concepts.key_idea: Equal temperature means no net heat flow -- and the zeroth law makes the thermometer legitimate.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph204.txt lines 30-140 (sections 11.2 thermal equilibrium, 11.3 zeroth law of thermodynamics, thermometer and variable like pressure used to sense temperature)
question_patterns: state the zeroth law of thermodynamics and its use

solution_steps.explain: In thermal equilibrium the macroscopic variables stop drifting and the net heat exchange is zero.
Equilibrium with a common third system forces equilibrium between any pair -- temperature equality is transitive.
A thermometer works because reading it is just testing equilibrium with a calibrated system.

concepts.title: Heat, Internal Energy and Work in a Gas
concepts.definition: A gas carries internal energy in the motion and interactions of its molecules. Two routes change it: heat, energy flowing because of temperature difference, and work, energy transferred by volume change against a piston. Neither heat nor work is a property of the state -- only internal energy is.
concepts.key_idea: Internal energy is a state property; heat and work are two roads into it, defined only during the journey.

solution_steps.explain: Heat into the gas and work done by the gas are taken positive.

solution_steps.action: read work from the pV diagram
solution_steps.explain: Work equals the area under the pressure-volume curve for the process taken.
The same internal energy change can be reached by many different heat and work splits -- only their sum is fixed.

concepts.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.definition: Energy bookkeeping for a gas: the change in internal energy equals the heat supplied to the system minus the work the system does on its surroundings. It is the law of conservation of energy applied to thermal systems, valid for every process whatever the path.
concepts.key_idea: Heat in either raises the internal energy or leaves as work done -- nothing vanishes.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph204.txt lines 261-350 (section 11.5 first law of thermodynamics, application to isothermal and adiabatic processes, specific heats of gases)

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the work done by the gas from the heat supplied to get the internal energy change.

concepts.title: Specific Heats of Gases and Mayer's Relation
concepts.definition: Heating a gas at constant volume spends energy only on internal energy (capacity Cv), while heating at constant pressure must also pay for expansion work, so Cp exceeds Cv. Their difference equals the universal gas constant R -- Mayer's relation -- and their ratio gamma controls adiabatic behaviour.
concepts.key_idea: Constant-pressure heating costs extra because the gas pushes the piston -- that extra is exactly R per mole.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph204.txt lines 300-420 (sections 11.6 specific heat capacity, 11.7 thermodynamic processes mentioning molar specific heats, Cp minus Cv equals R)
question_patterns: why is Cp greater than Cv for a gas
in class 11 thermodynamics: state Mayer's relation between Cp and Cv
define gamma and give typical values for mono and diatomic gases
find the heat needed to raise the gas temperature at constant volume
which specific heat applies to an isobaric heating of the gas
how does gamma influence the speed of sound in a gas

solution_steps.explain: No piston moves, so every joule goes into internal energy -- that defines Cv.
The gas must expand to keep pressure constant, spending extra energy as work -- that defines Cp.
Cp - Cv = R per mole, and gamma = Cp/Cv lies between 1 and about 1.67 for real gases.

concepts.title: Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
concepts.definition: In an isothermal change the temperature never shifts, so an ideal gas keeps pV constant and all absorbed heat leaves as work. In an adiabatic change no heat crosses the wall at all, pressure and volume follow p times V gamma constant, and the gas cools on expansion and heats on compression entirely from its own internal energy.
concepts.key_idea: Isothermal trades heat for work; adiabatic trades internal energy for work -- the wall decides which.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph204.txt lines 380-500 (sections 11.8.2 isothermal process, 11.8.3 adiabatic process, pV diagrams, comparison of slopes)
question_patterns: compare isothermal and adiabatic processes on a pV diagram
in class 11 thermodynamics: why does an adiabatic expansion cool the gas
write the relation between pressure and volume for an adiabatic change
an ideal gas expands isothermally, what happens to the absorbed heat
which process has the steeper pV curve and why
give a real example of a nearly adiabatic compression

solution_steps.explain: Isothermal means perfect thermal contact with a reservoir; adiabatic means perfect insulation.
Isothermal keeps pV constant; adiabatic keeps p V^gamma constant, the extra gamma reflecting rising temperature on compression.
Isothermal: heat in equals work out with no temperature change. Adiabatic: work comes entirely from internal energy, so temperature moves.

concepts.title: Heat Engines, Carnot Efficiency and the Second Law
concepts.definition: A heat engine robs a hot reservoir of heat, turns part of it into work and dumps the remainder into a cold sink; efficiency is the work fraction of the absorbed heat. The best possible engine working between two temperatures is the reversible Carnot engine, whose efficiency depends only on those temperatures -- no engine can beat it, which is the second law's core message.
concepts.key_idea: Even perfect engines must reject heat -- efficiency is capped by one minus the temperature ratio of the sinks.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph204.txt lines 500-640 (sections 11.9 heat engines, 11.10 refrigerators, 11.11 Carnot engine, second law Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements)
question_patterns: find the efficiency of a heat engine from the work output and heat input

solution_steps.explain: Divide the cold reservoir temperature by the hot reservoir temperature, both in kelvin.
One minus that ratio is the maximum possible efficiency.
